newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania political deadlock, pyramid refunds begin.
newsitem.headline: Albania political deadlock, pyramid refunds begin.

text.p: Albania's rightist president is deadlocked with the opposition over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, but bankers say some 350,000 distraught investors will begin getting partial refunds on Tuesday.
President Sali Berisha called on 20 political groups to attend a round table on compensating depositors who ploughed life savings into the schemes in Europe's poorest country.

Opposition parties, newly united in a "Forum for Democracy", dismissed the meeting on Tuesday as a publicity stunt and said they had no intention of attending. Instead, they renewed demands for the government's resignation.

"The solution does not merely involve how to dispense money," the official ATA news agency quoted Ylli Bufi, a senior leader of the main opposition Socialist Party, as saying. "It means finding a way out of the crisis gripping our economy."

Virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million, lulled by promises of big returns, had committed funds to the schemes in the six years following the fall of eastern Europe's most repressive and isolationist communist regime.

Enraged investors set fire to buildings in protests against collapses last month. But nearly 150 arrests and threats of long jail terms on rioting charges cut short fresh protests last weekend as many would-be demonstrators stayed home.
Five schemes have folded in the past three months, but compensation has been announced only for two "charity foundations" whose assets were seized in state banks.
Two top bankers told state television that investors in the Populli scheme would get back 60 percent of their stake, starting on Tuesday, on production of proper documents.
Payments in a second scheme, Xhaferri, would start a day later. Depositors would be free to choose between cash or government certificates and could even later change their mind.
For the third day running, television broadcast appeals to shun violence - by Moslem, Orthodox and Roman Catholic clergy.
Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi told Radio Tirana after a cabinet meeting: "The message to investors is that they should remain calm. They will get their money."

The radio announced that 24 more demonstrators had been formally charged with public offences in the southern towns of Lushnje and Berat. It also said a top official in the Gjallica pyramid scheme in the south had been arrested on fraud charges.
A senior leader of Berisha's Democratic Party told a visiting Italian delegation that the government's stand "was the best choice and prevented a deterioration of events".
The party, first elected in 1992, backs market reforms in the Balkan country and until last year boasted one of the best records for growth among ex-communist countries.
It won a new term last year in polls criticised as unfair and rigged by Western observers and has free rein in a parliament largely boycotted by the opposition.

The Forum for Democracy, set up last week, brings together for the first time Berisha's disparate opponents, including leftists, centrists and former political prisoners, all dedicated to ousting Prime Minister Meksi.

The crisis has put pressure on Albania's lek currency, which has lost 30 percent of its value against the dollar since the New Year. Last week, it sank to 135 to the dollar, rallied at the weekend, but fell again on Monday to 120.
